## R Markdown

This is an R Markdown document. Markdown is a simple formatting syntax for authoring HTML, PDF, and MS Word documents. For more details on using R Markdown see <http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com>.

When you click the **Knit** button a document will be generated that includes both content as well as the output of any embedded R code chunks within the document. You can embed an R code chunk like this:

```{r cars}
summary(cars)
```

## Including Plots

You can also embed plots, for example:

```{r pressure, echo=FALSE}
plot(pressure)
```

Note that the `echo = FALSE` parameter was added to the code chunk to prevent printing of the R code that generated the plot.

```{r}
# TODO: Using the same a and b, compute and print a %% b and a %/% b
# a %% b = remainder of a / b
# a %/% b = whole-number (integer) division

b <- 5

a %/% b
```

## Part B - Basic Data Types

```{r}
# TODO: Use typeof() to check the type of each of x, y, z, w, v
x <- 42
y <- 42L       
z <- "42"
w <- TRUE
v <- 3 + 2i   

typeof(x)
typeof(y)
typeof(z)
typeof(w)
typeof(v)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Use class() to check the class of each of x, y, z, w, v
x <- 42
y <- 42L       
z <- "42"
w <- TRUE
v <- 3 + 2i   

class(x)
class(y)
class(z)
class(w)
class(v)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Use mode() to check the class of each of x, y, z, w, v
x <- 42
y <- 42L       
z <- "42"
w <- TRUE
v <- 3 + 2i   

mode(x)
mode(y)
mode(z)
mode(w)
mode(v)
```

```{r}
#Question 3: Answer
#The use of L in the variable y converts its value into an integer. x is declared as double by default in R language.

#Question #4: Answer
#typeof() checks the data type of the variable
#class() seems to check the values inside the variable based on its class.
#mode() seems to check the actual values inside the variable.
```

## Part C - Type Conversion

```{r}
# TODO: Convert num_string to a numeric value using as.numeric()
# Then check its type with typeof(), class(), and mode()
num_string <- "123"
as.numeric(num_string)

typeof(num_string)
class(num_string)
mode(num_string)
```

```{r}

1
as.logical(0)
as.logical(1)

```

## Part D - Strings, paste(), and paste0()

```{r}
# TODO: Print first_name and last_name using print() and/or cat()
first_name <- "Juan"
last_name <- "Dela Cruz"

print(first_name)
print(last_name)

cat(first_name, last_name, "\n")
```

```{r}
# TODO: Use paste() to combine first_name and last_name into a full name
# TODO: Use paste0() to do the same, and compare the two results

full_name <- paste(first_name, last_name)
print(full_name)

full_name0 <- paste0(first_name, last_name)
print(full_name0)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Use paste() with the argument sep = "-" to join first_name and
# last_name with a dash instead of a space

name_with_dash <- paste(first_name, last_name, sep = "-")
print(name_with_dash)
```

```{r}
age <- 21
# TODO: Use paste0() to build the sentence:
# "Juan Dela Cruz is 21 years old." by combining full_name, age, and text

sentence <- paste0(full_name, " is ", age, " years old.")
print(sentence)
```
